flawed_step: Step 1: the proposed implication from “triangle-free” to “3-colorable” cannot be justified. No numbered proof steps were supplied, and this first substantive claim is false.
counterexample: Use the 11-vertex Mycielski graph of C5. Its vertices are v0,...,v4, u0,...,u4, and w, with indices modulo 5. Its edges are vi-v(i+1), ui-v(i-1), ui-v(i+1), and w-ui for every i, with no other edges. Explicitly, the v-edges form v0-v1-v2-v3-v4-v0; u0 is adjacent to v4,v1; u1 to v0,v2; u2 to v1,v3; u3 to v2,v4; u4 to v3,v0; and w is adjacent to all five ui. It is triangle-free: the ui are independent, so a triangle containing w is impossible; a triangle among the vi is impossible because they induce C5; and a triangle containing exactly one ui would require v(i-1) and v(i+1) to be adjacent, which they are not in C5. It is not 3-colorable. Suppose c were a proper 3-coloring and rename colors so c(w)=3. Every ui then has color 1 or 2. Define a 2-coloring d of the underlying C5 by d(vi)=c(vi) when c(vi) is not 3, and d(vi)=c(ui) when c(vi)=3. For every C5 edge vi-vj, its endpoints cannot both have color 3. If neither does, their d-colors differ because c is proper. If, say, c(vi)=3, then ui is adjacent to vj, so c(ui) differs from c(vj), and again d(vi) differs from d(vj). Thus d would properly 2-color the odd cycle C5, which is impossible. Hence this explicit triangle-free graph requires at least four colors.
assessment_summary: The claim is false. The explicitly specified 11-vertex Mycielski graph is triangle-free but admits no proper coloring with three colors.
